Stress:

The restoring force acting per unit area of deforming body.

Stress$ = \dfrac{F_{\text{external}} \text{ (at equilibrium)}}{A}$

SI unit$:N/m² $     Dimensions:  $\left[\mathrm{M}^1 \mathrm{~L}^{-1} \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]$

Types of stress:

1.Longitudinal Stress: When the force acts normal to the cross-section area then stress produced is called longitudinal stress.

Longitudinal Stress $= \dfrac{F_{\perp}}{A}$

There are two types of longitudinal stress

(a)Tensile Stress:

The longitudinal stress, produced due to increase in the length of a body.

(b)Compressive Stress:

The longitudinal stress, produced due to the decrease in the length of a body.

2.Volume Stress/Hydraulic Stress: When forces act on a body’s surface such that (a) they are normal to the surface and (b) their magnitude is proportional to the area, The force opposing this change in volume per unit area produces a stress defined as volumetric stress.

Volume Stress/Hydraulic Stress $ = \dfrac{F_{\perp}}{A}$$=P$

3.Shear Stress/Tangential Stress: When force is tangential or parallel to surface of a body then stress produced is known as shear stress.  Due to this stress, the shape of the body changes or it gets twisted but not its volume.

Shear Stress/Tangential Stress = $\frac{F_t}{A} $ = $\frac{F_{\text{Tangential}}}{A}$

4.Breaking Stress:

The minimum stress required to cause the actual fracture of a material is called the breaking stress or ultimate strength.

Breaking stress $=\dfrac{\mathrm{F}_{\max }}{\mathrm{A}} $

$\mathrm{~F}_{\max }$ = force required to break the body.

Strain and Its Types:

Strain $ = \dfrac{\text{Change in the dimension of the body}}{\text{Original dimension of the body}}$

It is a unitless and dimensionless quantity

(1) Longitudinal strain:

Longitudinal strain $=\dfrac{\text { change in length of the body }}{\text { initial length of the body }}$

Longitudinal strain $=\dfrac{\Delta \mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{~L}}$

(2) Volumetric strain:

$\text { Volume strain }=\dfrac{\text { change in volume of the body }}{\text { original volume of the body }}$

Volume strain  $=\dfrac{\Delta \mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{~V}}$

(3) Shear strain:

When applied force is parallel to cross-section, shape changes$$

$\tan \phi=\dfrac{x}{L} \text { (Here } \phi \text { is very small) }$

$\tan \phi=\dfrac{x}{L}=\dfrac{\text {displacement of upper face relative to the lower face }}{\text {distance between two faces }}$

Relation between Angle of Twist and Angle of Shear:

When a cylinder of length $L$ and radius $r$ is fixed at one end and a tangential force is applied at the other end, then the cylinder gets twisted.

$r \theta = L \phi$

$\phi = \dfrac{r \theta}{L}$

$\theta = \text{Angle of twist}$

$\phi = \text{Angle of shear}$

Hooke's Law: According to this law within the elastic limit the stress produced in a body is directly proportional to the corresponding strain.

Stress $\propto$ Strain or  Stress = E × strain

Here, E = coefficient of elasticity or modulus of elasticity

$E = \dfrac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}}$

The slope of stress & strain graph gives coefficient of elasticity.

Significance of Modulus of Elasticity:

More is the value of Modulus of Elasticity, more is the Elasticity of material.

(A) E depends on :-

1. Nature of material

2. Impurities

3. Temperature

(B) E independent from:-

1. Stress

2. Strain

Young's Modulus of Elasticity: Within elastic limit, the ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain.

$Y = \dfrac{\text{Longitudinal Stress}}{\text{Longitudinal Strain}}$

$Y = \dfrac{F L}{A \Delta L}$

Bulk modulus of elasticity 'K' or 'B': Within elastic limit, the ratio of the volumetric stress (i.e., change in pressure) to the volumetric strain.

$K \, \text{or} \, B = \dfrac{\text{Volumetric Stress}}{\text{Volumetric Strain}}$

$K \, \text{or} \, B = \dfrac{\Delta P}{-\dfrac{\Delta V}{V}}$

Compressibility: The reciprocal of Bulk modulus of elasticity.

$C = \dfrac{1}{K}$

Modulus of Rigidity '$\eta$ '

Within elastic limit, the ratio of shearing stress to shearing strain is called modulus of rigidity of a material.

Note: Angle of shear  $ \Phi $  is always taken in radians

$\eta=\dfrac{\text { shearing stress }}{\text { shearing strain }}=\left(\dfrac{\dfrac{F_{\text {tangential }}}{A}}{\phi}\right)=\dfrac{F_{\text {tangential }}}{A \phi}$

blocks.text:
Fluid: Fluids are the substances that can flow or deforms. Therefore, liquids and gases both are fluids.

Density$(\rho)$ :

$\text{Density} = \dfrac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Volume}}$

$\text { Units - } \dfrac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{~m}^3} \text { (SI system) }$

Density Of Mixture :

If two immiscible liquids of mass m1 and m2 and volume V1 and V2 are mixed together then density of mixture is given by :

$\rho_{\text{mix}}$\ = \dfrac{\text{Total mass of mixture}}{\text{Total Volume of mixture}}$=\dfrac{m_1 + m_2}{v_1 + v_2}$$=\dfrac{m_1 + m_2}{\dfrac{m_1}{\rho_1} + \dfrac{m_2}{\rho_2}}$

Case(1) If liquid with same masses are mixed i.e. m1 =m2 = m then -

$\rho_{\text{mix}} = \dfrac{2 \rho_1 \rho_2}{\rho_1 + \rho_2}$

Case(2) If liquid with same volumes are mixed i.e. V1 = V2 = V then -

$\rho_{\text{mix}} = \dfrac{\rho_1 + \rho_2}{2}$

Relative Density :

$\text{Relative Density} = \dfrac{\text{Density of substance}}{\text{Density of pure water at } 4^\circ \text{C}}$

R.D is an unitless and dimensionless quantity.

Specific Weight :

$\text{Specific Weight} = \dfrac{\text{Weight of substance}}{\text{Volume of substance}}$$=\frac{mg}{V} = \rho g$

$Unit-\dfrac{\text{N}}{\text{m}^3}$

Specific Gravity :

$\text{Specific Gravity} = \dfrac{\text{Specific weight of substance}}{\text{Specific weight of pure water at } 4^\circ \text{C}}$$=\dfrac{\rho \ g}{\rho_{\text{w}} \c g}$=$\dfrac{\rho}{\rho_{\text{w}}}$=$R.D.$

Note: The numerical value of specific gravity and relative density are same.

Pressure: Pressure P is defined as the magnitude of the normal force acting per unit surface area.

$\mathrm{P}=\dfrac{\mathrm{F}_{\perp}}{\mathrm{A}} \text {, here } \mathrm{F}_{\perp}=\text { normal force on a surface of area } \mathrm{A}$

$\text { SI UNIT : Pascal (Pa) ; } 1 \mathrm{~Pa}=1 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^2 $

$\text { Dimensions : }\left[\mathrm{ML}^{-1} \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Types of Pressures

1. Atmospheric Pressure:

Force exerted by atmospheric column on unit cross-sectional area at mean sea level is called atmospheric pressure (P0).

$P_0 = 101.3 \, \text{kN/m}^2$

$P_0 = 1.013 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/m}^2$

Note: Barometer is used to measure the atmospheric pressure.

2. Gauge Pressure:

Excess Pressure over the atmospheric pressure ($P - P_{\text{atm}}$) measured with the help of pressure measuring instruments is called gauge pressure.

Note:  Gauge pressure is always measured with the help of a "manometer".

3. Absolute Pressure:

Sum of the atmospheric and gauge pressure is called absolute pressure.

$P_{\text{abs}} = P_{\text{atm}} + P_{\text{gauge}}$

$P_{\text{abs}} = P_0 + h \rho g$

Pressure due to liquid at depth 'h'

m = mass of liquid element

A = Area of cross - section of liquid element

Since fluid is at rest

$P_1 A + mg = P_2 A$

$P_1 A + (A h \rho) g = P_2 A$

$P_2 = P_1 + \rho g h$

Note:  Pressure exerted by a same liquid at any point does not depend on shape and size of the container (it means quantity of liquid). It depends only on the height of liquid column.

Pressure due to liquid on a vertical wall of container$=\dfrac{\rho g h}{2}$

Barometer:-  It Measure atmospheric pressure.

$\text { Atmospheric pressure } P_0=\rho g h=13.6 \times 10^3 \times 9.81 \times 76 \times 10^{-2}=1.013 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^2$

Case(1): Lift accelerating upwards with acceleration 'a'$=P_{\text{atm}} = \rho (g + a) h$

Case(2):Lift accelerating downwards with acceleration 'a'$=P_{\text{atm}} = \rho (g - a) h$

U-Tube Concept:

For the same stationary liquid, pressure at same horizontal level remains same.

$P_A = P_B$

$P_0 + h_{\text{Hg}} \rho_{\text{Hg}} g = P_0 + h_{\text{w}} \rho_{\text{w}} g$

$h_{\text{Hg}} \rho_{\text{Hg}} = h_{\text{w}} \rho_{\text{w}}$

Pascal's Law: This law states that when a change in pressure is applied to an enclosed fluid, it is transmitted undiminished to all portions of the fluid and to the walls of its container.

Applications of pascal's law :

Hydraulic lift:

$\dfrac{F_1}{A_1} = \dfrac{F_2}{A_2}$

$F_2 = \dfrac{A_2}{A_1} \times F_1$

blocks.text:
Archimedes Principle: It states that the upward buoyant force on a body that is partially or totally immersed in a fluid is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by it.

Net Upward Force

$F_2 - F_1 = A \sigma g (h_2 - h_1)$

$F = A \sigma g L = V_{\text{in}} \sigma g$

$V_{\text{in}}$=Volume of the body submerged in the fluid.

$AL$=Volume of displaced liquid

$mg$=Weight of displaced liquid

Apparent Weight:

$W_{\text{app}} = W - F_b \\ W_{\text{app}} = mg - V \sigma g \\ W_{\text{app}} = V \rho g - V \sigma g = V (\rho - \sigma) g$

$\text{Relative density} = \dfrac{W}{W - W_{\text{app}}}$

$\dfrac{\rho_s}{\rho_l}$=$ \dfrac{W}{W - W_{\text{app}}}$

Principle of Flotation:

Case 1: Density of the body is greater than that of liquid $(\rho > \sigma)$

In this case $W > F_b$

So the body will sink to the bottom of the liquid.

$W_{\text{app}} = W - F_b$=$V \rho g - V \sigma g$=V \rho g \left( 1 - \dfrac{\sigma}{\rho} \right)$=W \left( 1 - \dfrac{\sigma}{\rho} \right)$

Case 2: Density of the body is equal to the density of liquid $(\rho = \sigma)$

In this case $W = F_b$

So the body will float fully submerged in the liquid. It will be in neutral equilibrium

$W_{\text{app}} = W - F_b$$=0$

Case 3:Density of the body is lesser than that of liquid $(\rho < \sigma)$

In this case $W < F_b$

So the body will float partially submerged in the liquid. In this case the volume of liquid displaced by the body (Vin) will be less than the volume of body (V). This ensures that up thrust equals to W.

$W_{\text{app}} = W - F_b$$=0$

blocks.answer:

  • Volume of Metal ($V_{\text{metal}}$):

  • Density of Metal ($\rho_{\text{metal}}$):
$\rho_{\text{metal}} = \frac{30/9.8}{0.00102} \approx 2941 \, \text{kg/m}^3$

Types of Fluid Flow

Steady Flow: Fluid velocity at a point remains constant over time. Particles follow the same path (streamline), which cannot intersect.

Laminar Flow: Fluid particles move smoothly along parallel streamlines with consistent direction, but varying magnitudes.

Turbulent Flow: Irregular flow with zig-zag particle motion, causing energy losses and eddy formation.

Rotational Flow: Fluid particles rotate around their own axes while flowing.

Irrotational Flow: Particles do not rotate around their axes during flow.

Equation of Continuity

The continuity equation is the mathematical expression of the law of conservation of mass in fluid dynamics.

$\mathrm{A}_1 \mathrm{~V}_1=\mathrm{A}_2 \mathrm{~V}_2 \text { or } \quad \mathrm{Av}=\text { constant }$

$\text { Volume flux }=\text { Rate of flow }=\text { Volume of liquid flowing per second } \\ Q=\dfrac{d V}{d t}=A v$

$\text { Unit of }(Q) ; m^3 / \mathrm{s} \text { or } \dfrac{\text { Litre }}{\mathrm{sec}} \text { or } \dfrac{\mathrm{m} \ell}{\mathrm{~s}}$

Bernoulli's Equation: According to Bernoulli's Theorem, in case of steady flow of incompressible and non-viscous fluid through a tube of non-uniform cross section then the sum of the pressure energy per unit volume, the potential energy per unit volume and the kinetic energy per unit volume is same at every point in the tube, i.e.

$P + \dfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho gh = \text{constant}$ (Energy per unit volume)

$\dfrac{\mathrm{P}}{\rho}+\dfrac{v^2}{2}+g h=\text { constant }$ (Energy per unit mass)

$\dfrac{\mathrm{P}}{\rho g}+\dfrac{v^2}{2 g}+h=\text { constant }$(Energy per unit Weight)

$\dfrac{\mathrm{P}}{\rho \mathrm{~g}} \text { is called the pressure head }$

$\dfrac{v^2}{2 g} \text { is called the velocity head }$

h is called the gravitational/potential head.

  • Assumptions: Ideal, non-viscous, incompressible fluid, steady flow.
  • Applications: Describes pressure change with velocity/height differences.
Torricelli's law (Speed of Efflux):

area of cross-section of the vessel >>>  area of cross-section of the orifice

so  $\ V_A ~= 0$

$V_B = \sqrt{2gh}$ (This equation is same as that of the velocity acquired by a freely falling body after falling through h height and is known as Torricelli's law)

Reaction force on vessel: By Newton's third law : $F = \rho A v^2$

Venturimeter: Venturimeter is used to measure the flow velocities in an incompressible fluid.

If Q be the volume of liquid flowing per unit time then

$Q = A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$

$Q = A_1 A_2 \sqrt{\dfrac{2gh}{A_1^2 - A_2^2}}$

At a point where the cross-sectional area is smaller velocity is greater and pressure is lower and vice versa.

Applications of Bernoulli's Theory :-

• Magnus Effect (Observed in a Spinning Ball)
    • Sprayer or Atomizer
    • Motion of the Ping-Pong Ball
    • Blowing-off of Tin Roof Tops in Wind Storm
    • Pull-in or Attraction Force by Fast Moving Trains

blocks.question: Water is moving with a speed of 5 m/sec through a pipe with cross sectional area of 4cm2. The water gradually descends 10m as the pipe increase in area to 5cm2. If the pressure at the upper level is 2 atm then find the pressure at lower level. (g =10 m/s2)
blocks.answer:
$A_1 = 4 \, \text{cm}^2$,$A_2 = 5 \, \text{cm}^2$

$h_1 - h_2 = 10 \, \text{m}$

$v_1 = 5 \, \text{m/s}$

From Equation of Continuity

$A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$

$(4)(5) = 5 v_2$

$v_2 = 4 \, \text{m/s}$

Applying Bernoulli's Theorem-

$P_1 + \frac{1}{2} \rho v_1^2 + \rho g h_1 = P_2 + \frac{1}{2} \rho v_2^2 + \rho g h_2$

$P_2 = P_1 + \frac{1}{2} \rho \left( v_1^2 - v_2^2 \right) + \rho g \left( h_1 - h_2 \right)$

$P_2 = (2 \times 10^5) + \frac{1}{2} \times (10^3) \left( 5^2 - 4^2 \right) + 10^3 \times (10) \times (10)$

$P_2 = 2 \times 10^5 + 4.5 + 10^3 + 1 \times 10^5 = 3.045 \, \text{atm}$

blocks.title: CORE CONCEPTS
blocks.text:
• Surface Tension: Surface tension is basically a property of liquid. The liquid surface behaves like a stretched elastic membrane which has a natural tendency to contract and tends to have a minimum possible area.

(1) Cohesive Force: The force of attraction acting between the molecules of same material.

(2) Adhesive Force: The force of attraction acting between molecules of two different materials.

Mathematical Formula Surface Tension

$T = \dfrac{F}{L}$

SI Unit : $\dfrac{N}{m}$

Bodies on Liquid Surface

Floatation of bodies due to surface tension

(1) When a needle floats on the liquid surface then $2T \ell \sin \theta = Mg$

Maximum mass of needle which can float on the liquid surface

$M_{\text{max}} = \dfrac{2 T \ell}{g}$

(2) If the needle is lifted from the liquid surface then required excess force will be $F_{\text{excess}} = 2 T \ell$

$F_{\text{min}} = Mg + 2 T \ell$

(3) Required excess force for a square frame of side

$F_{\text{excess}} = 8 T \times \ell$

(4) Required excess force for a square lamina of side $\ell$

$F_{\text{excess}} = 4 T \times \ell$

(5) Required excess force for a rectangular frame of length $l$ width $b$  $F_{\text{excess}} = 4 T (l + b)$

(6) Required excess force for a rectangular lamina of length $\ell$ width $b$

$F_{\text{excess}} = 2T (\ell + b)$

(7) Required excess force for a circular thick ring (or annular ring) having internal and external radii  $r_ 1 $and $r _2$ is dipped in and taken out from liquid.

Surface Energy:

$S \cdot E \cdot=W=T(\Delta A)$

Special Cases:

Work done in blowing of small drop of radius $r_1$to large drop of radius $r_2, W=4 \pi T\left(r_2^2-r_1^2\right)$

• Work done in blowing of small bubble of radius $r_1$ to large bubble of radius $r_2, W=8 \pi T\left(r_2^2-r_1^2\right)$

• Work done (surface energy) in formation of a drop of radius $\mathrm{r}, W=4 \pi r^2 T$

• Work done (surface energy) in blowing of a soap bubble of radius r, $W=8 \pi r^2 T$

Splitting of big drop into smaller droplets :

$\dfrac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{R}^3=\mathrm{n}\left[\dfrac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{r}^3\right] \Rightarrow \mathrm{n}=\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{r}}\right]^3 \Rightarrow \mathrm{r}=\dfrac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{n}^{\dfrac{1}{3}}}$

Magnitude of work done against surface tension

$\mathrm{W}=4 \pi \mathrm{~T}\left(\mathrm{nr}^2-\mathrm{R}^2\right)=4 \pi \mathrm{R}^2 \mathrm{~T}\left(\mathrm{n}^{1 / 3}-1\right)=4 \pi \mathrm{R}^2 \mathrm{~T}\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{r}}-1\right] \Rightarrow \mathrm{W}=4 \pi \mathrm{R}^3 \mathrm{~T}\left[\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{r}}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}}\right]$

$\dfrac{(\mathrm{S} . \mathrm{E})_{\mathrm{f}}}{(\mathrm{~S} . \mathrm{E})_{\mathrm{i}}}=\mathrm{n}\left(\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{n}^{2 / 3}}\right)=\mathrm{n}^{1 / 3}$

In this process area increases, surface energy increases, internal energy decreases, temperature decreases, and energy is absorbed.

$\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{Jms} \Delta \theta=4 \pi \mathrm{R}^3 \mathrm{~T}\left[\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{r}}-\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}}\right] \Rightarrow \Delta \theta=\dfrac{3 \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{~J} \rho \mathrm{~s}}\left[\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{r}}-\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}}\right]$

Droplets are coalesce to form a big drop :

$|W|=4 \pi R^2 T\left(n^{1 / 3}-1\right)$

$\dfrac{(\mathrm{S} . \mathrm{E})_{\mathrm{f}}}{(\mathrm{~S} . \mathrm{E})_{\mathrm{i}}}=\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{n}^{1 / 3}}$

in this process surface area decreases, surface energy decreases, internal energy increases, temperature increases, and energy is released.

Excess Pressure in a Liquid Drop:

$\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{ex}}=\dfrac{2 \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{R}}$

Excess Pressure in a Soap Bubble:

$P_{e x}=\dfrac{4 T}{R}$

Special Cases:

(1) Two unequal soap bubbles are formed one on each side of a tube closed in the middle by a tap. When the tap is opened, then:-

$\begin{aligned} & P_A=P_0+\frac{4 T}{r} \\ & P_B=P_0+\frac{4 T}{R} \end{aligned}$

Clearly PA > PB ; so air will flow from A to B.

Ultimately bubble A becomes smaller and bubble B becomes bigger in size.

(2) Total pressure inside an air bubble in liquid

$P_{\text {in }}=P_0+\dfrac{2 T}{R}$

$\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathrm{P}_0+\rho \mathrm{gh}+\dfrac{2 \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{R}}$

(3) Total pressure inside a cavity or air bubble in liquid

$P_{\text {inside }}=P_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho \mathrm{gh}+\dfrac{2 T}{R}$

(4) If two bubbles of radii r1 and r2 coalesce isothermally in vacuum then the radius of the new bubble will be :

$\mathrm{r}=\sqrt{\mathrm{r}_1^2+\mathrm{r}_2^2}$

(5) If two bubbles of radii r1 and r2 (r1 < r2) come in contact with each other then the radius of curvature of the common surface

$\mathrm{r}=\dfrac{\mathrm{r}_1 \mathrm{r}_2}{\mathrm{r}_2-\mathrm{r}_1}$

Stress:

The restoring force acting per unit area of deforming body.

Stress$ = \dfrac{F_{\text{external}} \text{ (at equilibrium)}}{A}$

SI unit$:N/m² $     Dimensions:  $\left[\mathrm{M}^1 \mathrm{~L}^{-1} \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]$

Types of stress:

1.Longitudinal Stress: When the force acts normal to the cross-section area then stress produced is called longitudinal stress.

Longitudinal Stress $= \dfrac{F_{\perp}}{A}$

There are two types of longitudinal stress

(a)Tensile Stress:

The longitudinal stress, produced due to increase in the length of a body.

(b)Compressive Stress:

The longitudinal stress, produced due to the decrease in the length of a body.

2.Volume Stress/Hydraulic Stress: When forces act on a body’s surface such that (a) they are normal to the surface and (b) their magnitude is proportional to the area, The force opposing this change in volume per unit area produces a stress defined as volumetric stress.

Volume Stress/Hydraulic Stress $ = \dfrac{F_{\perp}}{A}$$=P$

3.Shear Stress/Tangential Stress: When force is tangential or parallel to surface of a body then stress produced is known as shear stress.  Due to this stress, the shape of the body changes or it gets twisted but not its volume.

Shear Stress/Tangential Stress = $\frac{F_t}{A} $ = $\frac{F_{\text{Tangential}}}{A}$

4.Breaking Stress:

The minimum stress required to cause the actual fracture of a material is called the breaking stress or ultimate strength.

Breaking stress $=\dfrac{\mathrm{F}_{\max }}{\mathrm{A}} $

$\mathrm{~F}_{\max }$ = force required to break the body.

Strain and Its Types:

Strain $ = \dfrac{\text{Change in the dimension of the body}}{\text{Original dimension of the body}}$

It is a unitless and dimensionless quantity

(1) Longitudinal strain:

Longitudinal strain $=\dfrac{\text { change in length of the body }}{\text { initial length of the body }}$

Longitudinal strain $=\dfrac{\Delta \mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{~L}}$

(2) Volumetric strain:

$\text { Volume strain }=\dfrac{\text { change in volume of the body }}{\text { original volume of the body }}$

Volume strain  $=\dfrac{\Delta \mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{~V}}$

(3) Shear strain:

When applied force is parallel to cross-section, shape changes$$

$\tan \phi=\dfrac{x}{L} \text { (Here } \phi \text { is very small) }$

$\tan \phi=\dfrac{x}{L}=\dfrac{\text {displacement of upper face relative to the lower face }}{\text {distance between two faces }}$

Relation between Angle of Twist and Angle of Shear:

When a cylinder of length $L$ and radius $r$ is fixed at one end and a tangential force is applied at the other end, then the cylinder gets twisted.

$r \theta = L \phi$

$\phi = \dfrac{r \theta}{L}$

$\theta = \text{Angle of twist}$

$\phi = \text{Angle of shear}$

Stress $\propto$ Strain or  Stress = E × strain

Here, E = coefficient of elasticity or modulus of elasticity

The slope of stress & strain graph gives coefficient of elasticity.

Significance of Modulus of Elasticity:

More is the value of Modulus of Elasticity, more is the Elasticity of material.

(A) E depends on :-

(B) E independent from:-

Young's Modulus of Elasticity: Within elastic limit, the ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain.

Bulk modulus of elasticity 'K' or 'B': Within elastic limit, the ratio of the volumetric stress (i.e., change in pressure) to the volumetric strain.

$K \, \text{or} \, B = \dfrac{\text{Volumetric Stress}}{\text{Volumetric Strain}}$

$K \, \text{or} \, B = \dfrac{\Delta P}{-\dfrac{\Delta V}{V}}$

Compressibility: The reciprocal of Bulk modulus of elasticity.

$C = \dfrac{1}{K}$

Modulus of Rigidity '$\eta$ '

blocks.text:
Fluid: Fluids are the substances that can flow or deforms. Therefore, liquids and gases both are fluids.

Density$(\rho)$ :

$\text{Density} = \dfrac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Volume}}$

$\text { Units - } \dfrac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{~m}^3} \text { (SI system) }$

Density Of Mixture :

If two immiscible liquids of mass m1 and m2 and volume V1 and V2 are mixed together then density of mixture is given by :

$\rho_{\text{mix}}$\ = \dfrac{\text{Total mass of mixture}}{\text{Total Volume of mixture}}$=\dfrac{m_1 + m_2}{v_1 + v_2}$$=\dfrac{m_1 + m_2}{\dfrac{m_1}{\rho_1} + \dfrac{m_2}{\rho_2}}$

Case(1) If liquid with same masses are mixed i.e. m1 =m2 = m then -

$\rho_{\text{mix}} = \dfrac{2 \rho_1 \rho_2}{\rho_1 + \rho_2}$

Case(2) If liquid with same volumes are mixed i.e. V1 = V2 = V then -

$\rho_{\text{mix}} = \dfrac{\rho_1 + \rho_2}{2}$

Relative Density :

$\text{Relative Density} = \dfrac{\text{Density of substance}}{\text{Density of pure water at } 4^\circ \text{C}}$

R.D is an unitless and dimensionless quantity.

Specific Weight :

$\text{Specific Weight} = \dfrac{\text{Weight of substance}}{\text{Volume of substance}}$$=\frac{mg}{V} = \rho g$

$Unit-\dfrac{\text{N}}{\text{m}^3}$

Specific Gravity :

$\text{Specific Gravity} = \dfrac{\text{Specific weight of substance}}{\text{Specific weight of pure water at } 4^\circ \text{C}}$$=\dfrac{\rho \ g}{\rho_{\text{w}} \c g}$=$\dfrac{\rho}{\rho_{\text{w}}}$=$R.D.$

Note: The numerical value of specific gravity and relative density are same.

Pressure: Pressure P is defined as the magnitude of the normal force acting per unit surface area.

$\mathrm{P}=\dfrac{\mathrm{F}_{\perp}}{\mathrm{A}} \text {, here } \mathrm{F}_{\perp}=\text { normal force on a surface of area } \mathrm{A}$

$\text { SI UNIT : Pascal (Pa) ; } 1 \mathrm{~Pa}=1 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^2 $

$\text { Dimensions : }\left[\mathrm{ML}^{-1} \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Types of Pressures

1. Atmospheric Pressure:

Force exerted by atmospheric column on unit cross-sectional area at mean sea level is called atmospheric pressure (P0).

$P_0 = 101.3 \, \text{kN/m}^2$

$P_0 = 1.013 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/m}^2$

Note: Barometer is used to measure the atmospheric pressure.

2. Gauge Pressure:

Excess Pressure over the atmospheric pressure ($P - P_{\text{atm}}$) measured with the help of pressure measuring instruments is called gauge pressure.

Note:  Gauge pressure is always measured with the help of a "manometer".

3. Absolute Pressure:

Sum of the atmospheric and gauge pressure is called absolute pressure.

$P_{\text{abs}} = P_{\text{atm}} + P_{\text{gauge}}$

$P_{\text{abs}} = P_0 + h \rho g$

Pressure due to liquid at depth 'h'

m = mass of liquid element

A = Area of cross - section of liquid element

Since fluid is at rest

$P_1 A + mg = P_2 A$

$P_1 A + (A h \rho) g = P_2 A$

$P_2 = P_1 + \rho g h$

Note:  Pressure exerted by a same liquid at any point does not depend on shape and size of the container (it means quantity of liquid). It depends only on the height of liquid column.

Pressure due to liquid on a vertical wall of container$=\dfrac{\rho g h}{2}$

Barometer:-  It Measure atmospheric pressure.

$\text { Atmospheric pressure } P_0=\rho g h=13.6 \times 10^3 \times 9.81 \times 76 \times 10^{-2}=1.013 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^2$

Case(1): Lift accelerating upwards with acceleration 'a'$=P_{\text{atm}} = \rho (g + a) h$

Case(2):Lift accelerating downwards with acceleration 'a'$=P_{\text{atm}} = \rho (g - a) h$

U-Tube Concept:

For the same stationary liquid, pressure at same horizontal level remains same.

$P_A = P_B$

$P_0 + h_{\text{Hg}} \rho_{\text{Hg}} g = P_0 + h_{\text{w}} \rho_{\text{w}} g$

$h_{\text{Hg}} \rho_{\text{Hg}} = h_{\text{w}} \rho_{\text{w}}$

Pascal's Law: This law states that when a change in pressure is applied to an enclosed fluid, it is transmitted undiminished to all portions of the fluid and to the walls of its container.

Applications of pascal's law :

Hydraulic lift:

$F_2 = \dfrac{A_2}{A_1} \times F_1$

blocks.title: CORE CONCEPTS
blocks.text:
Archimedes Principle: It states that the upward buoyant force on a body that is partially or totally immersed in a fluid is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by it.

Net Upward Force

$F_2 - F_1 = A \sigma g (h_2 - h_1)$

$F = A \sigma g L = V_{\text{in}} \sigma g$

$V_{\text{in}}$=Volume of the body submerged in the fluid.

$AL$=Volume of displaced liquid

$mg$=Weight of displaced liquid

Apparent Weight:

$W_{\text{app}} = W - F_b \\ W_{\text{app}} = mg - V \sigma g \\ W_{\text{app}} = V \rho g - V \sigma g = V (\rho - \sigma) g$

$\text{Relative density} = \dfrac{W}{W - W_{\text{app}}}$

$\dfrac{\rho_s}{\rho_l}$=$ \dfrac{W}{W - W_{\text{app}}}$

Principle of Flotation:

Case 1: Density of the body is greater than that of liquid $(\rho > \sigma)$

In this case $W > F_b$

So the body will sink to the bottom of the liquid.

$W_{\text{app}} = W - F_b$=$V \rho g - V \sigma g$=V \rho g \left( 1 - \dfrac{\sigma}{\rho} \right)$=W \left( 1 - \dfrac{\sigma}{\rho} \right)$

Case 2: Density of the body is equal to the density of liquid $(\rho = \sigma)$

In this case $W = F_b$

So the body will float fully submerged in the liquid. It will be in neutral equilibrium

$W_{\text{app}} = W - F_b$$=0$

Case 3:Density of the body is lesser than that of liquid $(\rho < \sigma)$

In this case $W < F_b$

So the body will float partially submerged in the liquid. In this case the volume of liquid displaced by the body (Vin) will be less than the volume of body (V). This ensures that up thrust equals to W.

$W_{\text{app}} = W - F_b$$=0$

blocks.title: CORE CONCEPTS
blocks.text:
Types of Fluid Flow

Steady Flow: Fluid velocity at a point remains constant over time. Particles follow the same path (streamline), which cannot intersect.

Laminar Flow: Fluid particles move smoothly along parallel streamlines with consistent direction, but varying magnitudes.

Turbulent Flow: Irregular flow with zig-zag particle motion, causing energy losses and eddy formation.

Rotational Flow: Fluid particles rotate around their own axes while flowing.

Irrotational Flow: Particles do not rotate around their axes during flow.

Equation of Continuity

The continuity equation is the mathematical expression of the law of conservation of mass in fluid dynamics.

$\mathrm{A}_1 \mathrm{~V}_1=\mathrm{A}_2 \mathrm{~V}_2 \text { or } \quad \mathrm{Av}=\text { constant }$

$\text { Volume flux }=\text { Rate of flow }=\text { Volume of liquid flowing per second } \\ Q=\dfrac{d V}{d t}=A v$

$\text { Unit of }(Q) ; m^3 / \mathrm{s} \text { or } \dfrac{\text { Litre }}{\mathrm{sec}} \text { or } \dfrac{\mathrm{m} \ell}{\mathrm{~s}}$

Bernoulli's Equation: According to Bernoulli's Theorem, in case of steady flow of incompressible and non-viscous fluid through a tube of non-uniform cross section then the sum of the pressure energy per unit volume, the potential energy per unit volume and the kinetic energy per unit volume is same at every point in the tube, i.e.

$P + \dfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho gh = \text{constant}$ (Energy per unit volume)

$\dfrac{\mathrm{P}}{\rho}+\dfrac{v^2}{2}+g h=\text { constant }$ (Energy per unit mass)

$\dfrac{\mathrm{P}}{\rho g}+\dfrac{v^2}{2 g}+h=\text { constant }$(Energy per unit Weight)

$\dfrac{\mathrm{P}}{\rho \mathrm{~g}} \text { is called the pressure head }$

$\dfrac{v^2}{2 g} \text { is called the velocity head }$

h is called the gravitational/potential head.

  • Assumptions: Ideal, non-viscous, incompressible fluid, steady flow.
  • Applications: Describes pressure change with velocity/height differences.
Torricelli's law (Speed of Efflux):

area of cross-section of the vessel >>>  area of cross-section of the orifice

so  $\ V_A ~= 0$

$V_B = \sqrt{2gh}$ (This equation is same as that of the velocity acquired by a freely falling body after falling through h height and is known as Torricelli's law)

Reaction force on vessel: By Newton's third law : $F = \rho A v^2$

Venturimeter: Venturimeter is used to measure the flow velocities in an incompressible fluid.

If Q be the volume of liquid flowing per unit time then

$Q = A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$

$Q = A_1 A_2 \sqrt{\dfrac{2gh}{A_1^2 - A_2^2}}$

At a point where the cross-sectional area is smaller velocity is greater and pressure is lower and vice versa.

(2) Adhesive Force: The force of attraction acting between molecules of two different materials.

Mathematical Formula Surface Tension

$T = \dfrac{F}{L}$

SI Unit : $\dfrac{N}{m}$

Bodies on Liquid Surface

Floatation of bodies due to surface tension

(1) When a needle floats on the liquid surface then $2T \ell \sin \theta = Mg$

Maximum mass of needle which can float on the liquid surface

$M_{\text{max}} = \dfrac{2 T \ell}{g}$

(2) If the needle is lifted from the liquid surface then required excess force will be $F_{\text{excess}} = 2 T \ell$

$F_{\text{min}} = Mg + 2 T \ell$

(3) Required excess force for a square frame of side

$F_{\text{excess}} = 8 T \times \ell$

(4) Required excess force for a square lamina of side $\ell$

$F_{\text{excess}} = 4 T \times \ell$

(5) Required excess force for a rectangular frame of length $l$ width $b$  $F_{\text{excess}} = 4 T (l + b)$

(6) Required excess force for a rectangular lamina of length $\ell$ width $b$

$F_{\text{excess}} = 2T (\ell + b)$

(7) Required excess force for a circular thick ring (or annular ring) having internal and external radii  $r_ 1 $and $r _2$ is dipped in and taken out from liquid.

$F_{\text{excess}} = 2 \pi T (r_1 + r_2)$

(8) Required excess force for a circular ring $\left(r_1=r_2=r\right)$

$F_{\text{excess}} = 4 \pi R T$

(9) Required excess force for a circular disc ( $ r_1=0, r_2=r $ )

$F_{\text{excess}} = 2 \pi R T$

Dependency of Surface Tension

• On Cohesive Force
    • On Impurities
    • On Temperature
    • On Contamination

Effects of surface tension

• Small liquid drops and soap bubbles are spherical.
    • The hairs of the brush remain separated from each other inside water, but when the brush is taken out, the hairs stick together.
    • Floatation of needle on water.
    • Formation of lead shots.

blocks.text:
Surface Energy:

$S \cdot E \cdot=W=T(\Delta A)$

Special Cases:

Work done in blowing of small drop of radius $r_1$to large drop of radius $r_2, W=4 \pi T\left(r_2^2-r_1^2\right)$

• Work done in blowing of small bubble of radius $r_1$ to large bubble of radius $r_2, W=8 \pi T\left(r_2^2-r_1^2\right)$

• Work done (surface energy) in formation of a drop of radius $\mathrm{r}, W=4 \pi r^2 T$

• Work done (surface energy) in blowing of a soap bubble of radius r, $W=8 \pi r^2 T$

Splitting of big drop into smaller droplets :

$\dfrac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{R}^3=\mathrm{n}\left[\dfrac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{r}^3\right] \Rightarrow \mathrm{n}=\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{r}}\right]^3 \Rightarrow \mathrm{r}=\dfrac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{n}^{\dfrac{1}{3}}}$

Magnitude of work done against surface tension

$\mathrm{W}=4 \pi \mathrm{~T}\left(\mathrm{nr}^2-\mathrm{R}^2\right)=4 \pi \mathrm{R}^2 \mathrm{~T}\left(\mathrm{n}^{1 / 3}-1\right)=4 \pi \mathrm{R}^2 \mathrm{~T}\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{r}}-1\right] \Rightarrow \mathrm{W}=4 \pi \mathrm{R}^3 \mathrm{~T}\left[\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{r}}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}}\right]$

$\dfrac{(\mathrm{S} . \mathrm{E})_{\mathrm{f}}}{(\mathrm{~S} . \mathrm{E})_{\mathrm{i}}}=\mathrm{n}\left(\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{n}^{2 / 3}}\right)=\mathrm{n}^{1 / 3}$

In this process area increases, surface energy increases, internal energy decreases, temperature decreases, and energy is absorbed.

$\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{Jms} \Delta \theta=4 \pi \mathrm{R}^3 \mathrm{~T}\left[\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{r}}-\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}}\right] \Rightarrow \Delta \theta=\dfrac{3 \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{~J} \rho \mathrm{~s}}\left[\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{r}}-\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}}\right]$

Droplets are coalesce to form a big drop :

$|W|=4 \pi R^2 T\left(n^{1 / 3}-1\right)$

$\dfrac{(\mathrm{S} . \mathrm{E})_{\mathrm{f}}}{(\mathrm{~S} . \mathrm{E})_{\mathrm{i}}}=\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{n}^{1 / 3}}$

in this process surface area decreases, surface energy decreases, internal energy increases, temperature increases, and energy is released.

Excess Pressure in a Liquid Drop:

$\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{ex}}=\dfrac{2 \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{R}}$

Excess Pressure in a Soap Bubble:

$P_{e x}=\dfrac{4 T}{R}$

Special Cases:

(1) Two unequal soap bubbles are formed one on each side of a tube closed in the middle by a tap. When the tap is opened, then:-

$\begin{aligned} & P_A=P_0+\frac{4 T}{r} \\ & P_B=P_0+\frac{4 T}{R} \end{aligned}$

Clearly PA > PB ; so air will flow from A to B.

Ultimately bubble A becomes smaller and bubble B becomes bigger in size.

(2) Total pressure inside an air bubble in liquid

$P_{\text {in }}=P_0+\dfrac{2 T}{R}$

$\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathrm{P}_0+\rho \mathrm{gh}+\dfrac{2 \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{R}}$

(3) Total pressure inside a cavity or air bubble in liquid

$P_{\text {inside }}=P_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho \mathrm{gh}+\dfrac{2 T}{R}$

(4) If two bubbles of radii r1 and r2 coalesce isothermally in vacuum then the radius of the new bubble will be :

$\mathrm{r}=\sqrt{\mathrm{r}_1^2+\mathrm{r}_2^2}$

(5) If two bubbles of radii r1 and r2 (r1 < r2) come in contact with each other then the radius of curvature of the common surface

$\mathrm{r}=\dfrac{\mathrm{r}_1 \mathrm{r}_2}{\mathrm{r}_2-\mathrm{r}_1}$

blocks.text:
Angle of Contact (θC): The angle enclosed between the tangent plane at the liquid surface and the tangent plane at the solid surface at the point of contact inside the liquid is defined as the angle of contact. The angle of contact depends on the nature of the solid and liquid in contact.

Dependency of Angle of Contact

  • Effect of Temperature on angle of contact
  • Effect of Impurities on angle of contact
  • Effect of Water Proofing Agent
Capillary Tube and Capillarity: A glass tube with a fine bore and open at both ends is known as a capillary tube. The property by virtue of which a liquid rises or gets depressed in a capillary tube is known as capillarity. Rise or fall of liquid in tubes of narrow bore (capillary tube) is called capillary action

In Equilibrium:

$\mathrm{h}=\dfrac{2 \mathrm{~T} \cos \theta_{\mathrm{c}}}{\mathrm{r} \rho \mathrm{~g}}$

Special Points:

(1) Zurin's Law :The height of rise of liquid in a capillary tube is inversely proportional to the radius of the capillary tube.

$\mathrm{h} \propto \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{r}} \text { or } \mathrm{rh}=\text { constant }$

(2) Inside a satellite, water will rise upto the top level but will not overflow and shape of meniscus will be plane.

(3)If a capillary tube is dipped into a liquid and tilted at an angle $\alpha$ from vertical then the vertical height of the liquid column remains same whereas the length of liquid column in the capillary tube increases.

blocks.title: CORE CONCEPTS
blocks.text:
Newton's Law of Viscosity

$\mathrm{F}=\eta \mathrm{A} \dfrac{\Delta \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{x}}}{\Delta \mathrm{y}}$

Here, $\eta $ = coefficient of viscosity

SI UNITS : N – s m–2 = Pa-s = poiseuille (PI) = deca poise

CGS UNITS : dyne-s/cm2 = poise;           1 decapoise = 10 poise.

Dimensions : [M1L–1T–1]

Important points:

1. Viscosity of fluid depends only on the nature of fluid and is independent of area considered or velocity gradient.

2. Thin liquids like water, alcohol are less viscous than thick liquids like blood, glycerin, honey.

Stoke's Law: Stoke showed that if a small sphere of radius r is moving with a velocity v through a homogeneous stationary medium (liquid or gas), of viscosity h then the viscous force acting on the sphere is $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{v}}=6 \pi \eta \mathrm{rv} .$

Terminal Velocity:

When a solid sphere falls in a liquid, its increasing velocity is controlled by the viscous force due to liquid and hence it attains a constant velocity which is known as the terminal velocity (vT).

$\mathrm{Th}+\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{v}}=\mathrm{W} \Rightarrow \dfrac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{r}^3 \sigma \mathrm{~g}+6 \pi \eta \mathrm{rv} \mathrm{}_{\mathrm{T}}=\dfrac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{r}^3 \rho \mathrm{~g}$

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{T}}=\dfrac{2}{9} \frac{\mathrm{r}^2(\rho-\sigma)}{\eta} \mathrm{g}$

Poiseuille's Formula: Steady flow of liquid of viscosity ($\eta$) in a capillary tube of length (L) and radius (r) under a pressure difference (P) across it, the volume of liquid flowing per second is given by

$\mathrm{Q}=\dfrac{\mathrm{dV}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\dfrac{\pi \mathrm{Pr}^4}{8 \eta \mathrm{~L}}$
